claims.evidence: This is stated as established knowledge in the introduction.

claims.claim: An important source of these neurons is the ventrolateral rhombomere 1 (r1), where GABA- and glutamatergic neuron precursors are generated from a neuroepithelial region expressing a homeodomain (HD) transcription factor (TF) Nkx6-1 (Lahti et al., 2016; Waite et al., 2012).
claims.source: An important source of these neurons is the ventrolateral rhombomere 1 (r1), where GABA- and glutamatergic neuron precursors are generated from a neuroepithelial region expressing a homeodomain (HD) transcription factor (TF) Nkx6-1 (Lahti et al., 2016; Waite et al., 2012).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous studies.

claims.claim: The rV2 precursors give rise to GABAergic neurons in the posterior Substantia Nigra pars reticulata, Ventral Tegmental Area, Rostromedial Tegmental Nucleus, and Ventral Tegmental Nucleus, all important for various aspects of behavioural control (Lahti et al., 2016; Morello et al., 2020a).
claims.source: The rV2 precursors give rise to GABAergic neurons in the posterior Substantia Nigra pars reticulata, Ventral Tegmental Area, Rostromedial Tegmental Nucleus, and Ventral Tegmental Nucleus, all important for various aspects of behavioural control (Lahti et al., 2016; Morello et al., 2020a).
claims.evidence: This is supported by citations to previous work.

claims.claim: A failure in the differentiation of the rV2 GABAergic neurons in the embryonic mouse brain, caused by mutation of the Tal1 gene, results in robust behavioural changes in postnatal mice, including hyperactivity, impulsivity, hypersensitivity to reward and learning deficits (Morello et al., 2020a).
claims.source: A failure in the differentiation of the rV2 GABAergic neurons in the embryonic mouse brain, caused by mutation of the Tal1 gene, results in robust behavioural changes in postnatal mice, including hyperactivity, impulsivity, hypersensitivity to reward and learning deficits (Morello et al., 2020a).
claims.evidence: This is supported by a citation to a previous study.

claims.claim: The Nkx6-1 positive proliferative progenitors of rV2 give rise to postmitotic V2b-like GABAergic precursors expressing selector genes Tal1, Gata2, and Gata3, and V2a-like glutamatergic precursors expressing Vsx1 and Vsx2 (Achim et al., 2014; Joshi et al., 2009; Muroyama et al., 2005).
claims.source: The Nkx6-1 positive proliferative progenitors of rV2 give rise to postmitotic V2b-like GABAergic precursors expressing selector genes Tal1, Gata2, and Gata3, and V2a-like glutamatergic precursors expressing Vsx1 and Vsx2 (Achim et al., 2014; Joshi et al., 2009; Muroyama et al., 2005).
claims.evidence: This is supported by citations to previous studies.

claims.claim: In the absence of Tal1, Gata2, and Gata3 function, differentiation of all the rV2 precursors is directed to glutamatergic neuron types (Achim et al., 2012; Lahti et al., 2016).
claims.source: In the absence of Tal1, Gata2, and Gata3 function, differentiation of all the rV2 precursors is directed to glutamatergic neuron types (Achim et al., 2012; Lahti et al., 2016).
claims.evidence: This is supported by citations to previous studies.

claims.claim: Tal1, Gata2, and Gata3 also retain their expression in the mature GABAergic neurons.
claims.source: Tal1, Gata2, and Gata3 also retain their expression in the mature GABAergic neurons.
claims.evidence: This is stated as a known fact about these transcription factors.

claims.claim: Tal1, Gata2, and Gata3 TFs operate as fate selectors, possibly responsible for both the induction and maintenance of the GABAergic identity in the anterior ventrolateral brainstem.
claims.source: Thus, Tal1, Gata2, and Gata3 TFs operate as fate selectors, possibly responsible for both the induction and maintenance of the GABAergic identity in the anterior ventrolateral brainstem.
claims.evidence: This is an inference based on the expression patterns and loss-of-function data.

claims.claim: The rV2 cells were arranged on pseudotemporal axes representing differentiating GABAergic or glutamatergic lineages.
claims.source: We found that the rV2 cells were arranged on pseudotemporal axes representing differentiating GABAergic or glutamatergic lineages (Figure 1A, B).
claims.evidence: This is based on scRNA-seq data analysis and visualization shown in Figure 1.

claims.claim: The GABAergic and glutamatergic selector TF genes (Tal1, Gata2, Gata3, Vsx1, Vsx2, Lhx4) were strongly expressed in the post-mitotic precursors at lineage bifurcation point and at the start of the lineage branches.
claims.source: The GABAergic and glutamatergic selector TF genes (Tal1, Gata2, Gata3, Vsx1, Vsx2, Lhx4) were strongly expressed in the post-mitotic precursors at lineage bifurcation point and at the start of the lineage branches (Figure 1—figure supplement 1A).
claims.evidence: This is based on scRNA-seq expression data shown in the figure.

claims.claim: Open chromatin features largely reflected the gene expression in the ventral r1 and allowed placing the developing rV2 neurons in cell groups and in a pseudotemporal order.
claims.source: In conclusion, open chromatin features largely reflected the gene expression in the ventral r1 and allowed placing the developing rV2 neurons in cell groups and in a pseudotemporal order.
claims.evidence: This is a conclusion based on the integration of scATAC-seq and scRNA-seq data.

claims.claim: The Tal1 locus, ±50 kb of the TSS, contains genes Stil, Tal1, Pdzk1ip1, and Cyp4x1 and 20 scATAC-seq features.
claims.source: The Tal1 locus, ±50 kb of the TSS, contains genes Stil, Tal1, Pdzk1ip1, and Cyp4x1 and 20 scATAC-seq features (Figure 2A).
claims.evidence: This is based on genomic analysis and visualization in Figure 2A.

claims.claim: Accessibility of 15 out of the 107 features in the TAD containing the Tal1 gene was linked to the Tal1 expression (p-value <0.05).
claims.source: Accessibility of 15 out of the 107 features in the TAD containing the Tal1 gene was linked to the Tal1 expression (p-value <0.05) (Supplementary file 3, Tal1 cCREs).
claims.evidence: This is based on statistical analysis of feature-to-gene linkage.

claims.claim: The gain in the accessibility of Tal1 cCREs at +0.7 and +40 kb correlated temporally with the up-regulation of Tal1 mRNA levels, strongly increasing in the earliest GABAergic precursors (GA1) and maintained at a lower level in the more mature GABAergic precursor groups (GA2–GA6).
claims.source: For example, the gain in the accessibility of Tal1 cCREs at +0.7 and +40 kb correlated temporally with the up-regulation of Tal1 mRNA levels, strongly increasing in the earliest GABAergic precursors (GA1) and maintained at a lower level in the more mature GABAergic precursor groups (GA2–GA6), as well as Pdzk1ip1 mRNA expression, increasing transiently in the earliest GABAergic precursors (GA1) (Figure 2A, B).
claims.evidence: This is based on correlation analysis of chromatin accessibility and gene expression data shown in Figure 2.

claims.claim: The identified Tal1 promoter feature (Tal1 +0.7 kb cCRE) contains Tal1 midbrain and hindbrain-spinal cord enhancers characterized earlier (Bockamp et al., 1997; Sinclair et al., 1999).
claims.source: Notably, the identified Tal1 promoter feature (Tal1 +0.7 kb cCRE) contains Tal1 midbrain and hindbrain-spinal cord enhancers characterized earlier (Bockamp et al., 1997; Sinclair et al., 1999).
claims.evidence: This is based on comparison with previously characterized enhancers cited in the literature.

claims.claim: The Tal1 +40 kb cCRE corresponds to the previously characterized enhancer region driving expression in the midbrain and hindbrain (Ogilvy et al., 2007).
claims.source: The Tal1 +40 kb cCRE corresponds to the previously characterized enhancer region driving expression in the midbrain and hindbrain (Ogilvy et al., 2007).
claims.evidence: This is based on comparison with a previously characterized enhancer.

claims.claim: Enhancers at –3.8 and +15.1/16/16.4 kb of Tal1 have been shown to drive Tal1 expression in haematopoietic stem cells and erythrocytes (Göttgens et al., 2004; Supplementary file 4, Figure 2—figure supplement 1A).
claims.source: Enhancers at –3.8 and +15.1/16/16.4 kb of Tal1 have been shown to drive Tal1 expression in haematopoietic stem cells and erythrocytes (Göttgens et al., 2004; Supplementary file 4, Figure 2—figure supplement 1A).
claims.evidence: This is based on comparison with previously characterized enhancers.

claims.claim: Two Gata2 cCREs, at –3.7 and +0 kb, are located in the proximal regulatory and promoter regions, which have been earlier shown to function as Gata2 mid- and hindbrain expression enhancers (Nozawa et al., 2009).
claims.source: Of these, two Gata2 cCREs, at –3.7 and +0 kb, are located in the proximal regulatory and promoter regions, which have been earlier shown to function as Gata2 mid- and hindbrain expression enhancers (Nozawa et al., 2009), as well as critical Gata2 autoregulation elements in haematopoietic cells (Kobayashi-Osaki et al., 2005; Supplementary file 4, Figure 2—figure supplement 1B).
claims.evidence: This is based on comparison with previously characterized enhancers.

claims.claim: An intronic Gata2 cCRE at +11.6 kb may mediate the regulation of Gata2 expression in the spinal cord V2 interneurons by Gata2–Tal1 co-binding (Joshi et al., 2009).
claims.source: We also identified an intronic Gata2 cCRE at +11.6 kb that may mediate the regulation of Gata2 expression in the spinal cord V2 interneurons by Gata2–Tal1 co-binding (Joshi et al., 2009).
claims.evidence: This is a speculation based on comparison with a previous study.

claims.claim: The Gata2 +22, +25.3, and +32.8 kb cCREs were accessible in the early precursors, before the opening of the Gata2 –3.7 kb cCRE in GA1 and Gata2 +0 kb cCRE in GA3–GA6.
claims.source: The Gata2 +22, +25.3, and +32.8 kb cCREs were accessible in the early precursors, before the opening of the Gata2 –3.7 kb cCRE in GA1 and Gata2 +0 kb cCRE in GA3–GA6 (Figure 2—figure supplement 2B, Supplementary file 3).
claims.evidence: This is based on temporal analysis of chromatin accessibility data.

claims.claim: The Gata3 +0.6 and +2.2 kb and the five upstream cCREs locate within the previously identified Gata3 CNS enhancer region (Lakshmanan et al., 1999).
claims.source: The Gata3 +0.6 and +2.2 kb and the five upstream cCREs locate within the previously identified Gata3 CNS enhancer region (Lakshmanan et al., 1999), and two of those also match Gata3 lens expression enhancers (Martynova et al., 2018; Supplementary file 4, Figure 2—figure supplement 1C).
claims.evidence: This is based on comparison with previously characterized enhancers.

claims.claim: The Gata3 +11.1 kb cCRE corresponds to the Gata3 proximal enhancer driving expression in PNS regions (Lieuw et al., 1997).
claims.source: The Gata3 +11.1 kb cCRE corresponds to the Gata3 proximal enhancer driving expression in PNS regions (Lieuw et al., 1997).
claims.evidence: This is based on comparison with a previously characterized enhancer.

claims.claim: The Gata3 +17.2 kb cCRE is located in the introns 3 and 4 of the Gata3 gene and may have enhancer activity in spinal cord V2b interneurons (Joshi et al., 2009; Supplementary file 4, Figure 2—figure supplement 1C).
claims.source: The Gata3 +17.2 kb cCRE is located in the introns 3 and 4 of the Gata3 gene and may have enhancer activity in spinal cord V2b interneurons (Joshi et al., 2009; Supplementary file 4, Figure 2—figure supplement 1C).
claims.evidence: This is a speculation based on comparison with a previous study.

claims.claim: The accessibility of the cCREs of the GABAergic selector TF genes changed with different kinetics during neuronal differentiation.
claims.source: Importantly, the accessibility of the cCREs of the GABAergic selector TF genes changed with different kinetics during neuronal differentiation.
claims.evidence: This is based on temporal analysis of chromatin accessibility data.

claims.claim: The accessibility of Tal1 +15.1, +16, +23, and Tal1 +40 kb cCREs was robustly detected before and at the onset of GABAergic differentiation and declined thereafter.
claims.source: For example, the accessibility of Tal1 +15.1, +16, +23, and Tal1 +40 kb cCREs was robustly detected before and at the onset of GABAergic differentiation and declined thereafter (Figure 2B).
claims.evidence: This is based on temporal analysis of chromatin accessibility data shown in Figure 2B.

claims.claim: The Tal1 +23 kb cCRE contained two scATAC-seq peaks, having temporally different patterns of accessibility.
claims.source: The Tal1 +23 kb cCRE contained two scATAC-seq peaks, having temporally different patterns of accessibility.
claims.evidence: This is based on detailed analysis of chromatin accessibility data.

claims.claim: The 3′ end of the Tal1 +23 kb feature contains binding sites of Nkx6-1 and Ascl1 that are expressed in the rV2 neuronal progenitors, while the 5′ end contains TF-binding sites of Insm1 and Tal1 TFs that are activated in early precursors.
claims.source: Detailed feature analysis indicated that the 3′ end of this feature contains binding sites of Nkx6-1 and Ascl1 that are expressed in the rV2 neuronal progenitors, while the 5′ end contains TF-binding sites of Insm1 and Tal1 TFs that are activated in early precursors (described below, see Figure 3C).
claims.evidence: This is based on footprinting analysis shown in Figure 3C.

claims.claim: The accessibility of the Tal1 +0.7 kb cCRE largely reflected the Tal1 mRNA expression and, unlike the early-peaking cCREs, such as Tal1 +40 kb, it was accessible also in the late GABAergic neuron precursors GA3–GA6.
claims.source: The accessibility of the Tal1 +0.7 kb cCRE largely reflected the Tal1 mRNA expression and, unlike the early-peaking cCREs, such as Tal1 +40 kb, it was accessible also in the late GABAergic neuron precursors GA3–GA6 (Figure 2B).
claims.evidence: This is based on correlation analysis of chromatin accessibility and gene expression data.

claims.claim: Distinct regulatory elements of the selector TFs may be responsible for the activation and for the maintenance of the lineage-specific expression of selector TF gene.
claims.source: Thus, distinct regulatory elements of the selector TFs may be responsible for the activation and for the maintenance of the lineage-specific expression of selector TF gene.
claims.evidence: This is an inference based on the different temporal patterns of cCRE accessibility.

claims.claim: Vsx2 gene expression was detected in the common precursors CO1 and increased in CO2 and the glutamatergic precursors (GL1–GL5).
claims.source: Vsx2 gene expression was detected in the common precursors CO1 and increased in CO2 and the glutamatergic precursors (GL1–GL5) (Figure 2C, RNA expression).
claims.evidence: This is based on scRNA-seq expression data shown in Figure 2C.

claims.claim: At the Vsx2 locus, an intronic feature (Vsx2 +20.5 kb) and the distal features at –61 and –21.3 kb of Vsx2 TSS were opened concomitant with its expression activation, whereas accessibility of the Vsx2 promoter region (Vsx2 +1.1 kb cCRE) and +27 kb cCRE increased later in the glutamatergic precursors.
claims.source: At the Vsx2 locus, an intronic feature (Vsx2 +20.5 kb) and the distal features at –61 and –21.3 kb of Vsx2 TSS were opened concomitant with its expression activation, whereas accessibility of the Vsx2 promoter region (Vsx2 +1.1 kb cCRE) and +27 kb cCRE increased later in the glutamatergic precursors (Figure 2D).
claims.evidence: This is based on temporal analysis of chromatin accessibility data shown in Figure 2D.

claims.claim: The Vsx2 r1 cCREs at –18.7, –21.3, +1.1, and +20.5 kb match previously characterized enhancers of Vsx2 expression in photoreceptor cells and retinal bipolar neurons and also contain putative autoregulatory Vsx2-binding sites occupied in developing spinal cord motor neuron and interneuron lineages.
claims.source: The information about the enhancers of Vsx2 brain expression is scarce, but our Vsx2 r1 cCREs at –18.7, –21.3, +1.1, and +20.5 kb match previously characterized enhancers of Vsx2 expression in photoreceptor cells and retinal bipolar neurons and also contain putative autoregulatory Vsx2-binding sites occupied in developing spinal cord motor neuron and interneuron lineages (Supplementary file 4, Figure 2—figure supplement 1D).
claims.evidence: This is based on comparison with previously characterized enhancers.

claims.claim: Odds ratios per chromosome were highest for exons and lowest for introns, odds ratios for features were between these two.
claims.source: Systematically, odds ratios per chromosome were highest for exons and lowest for introns, odds ratios for features were between these two.
claims.evidence: This is based on statistical analysis of sequence conservation.

claims.claim: All of the odds ratios showed a significant difference from what is expected if there was no relationship between the nucleotides within features and conservation (p = <2.20e−16, Fisher's exact test, Supplementary file 5, sheet per chromosome).
claims.source: All of the odds ratios showed a significant difference from what is expected if there was no relationship between the nucleotides within features and conservation (p = <2.20e−16, Fisher's exact test, Supplementary file 5, sheet per chromosome).
claims.evidence: This is based on statistical testing of sequence conservation.

claims.claim: The conservation of chromatin features is consistent with a putative role as regulatory sites.
claims.source: The conservation of chromatin features is consistent with a putative role as regulatory sites.
claims.evidence: This is an inference based on the conservation analysis.

claims.claim: The previously characterized enhancers, and especially the nervous system expression enhancers of Tal1, Gata2, Gata3, and Vsx2 mostly are found within the ATAC features identified here (63.6–100% of gene enhancers overlapping with scATAC-seq features, Figure 2—figure supplement 3B).
claims.source: Furthermore, literature research revealed that the previously characterized enhancers, and especially the nervous system expression enhancers of Tal1, Gata2, Gata3, and Vsx2 mostly are found within the ATAC features identified here (63.6–100% of gene enhancers overlapping with scATAC-seq features, Figure 2—figure supplement 3B).
claims.evidence: This is based on comparison of identified features with previously characterized enhancers.

claims.claim: Both Tal1 and Vsx2 cCREs contain conserved binding sites of Kr-like TFs, bHLH TFs, E2A, Ebf, E2F, NF-1, Pbx, and Sox TF families, and various HD TFs.
claims.source: We observed both common and distinct patterns of TF binding in the cCREs of Tal1 and Vsx2 in the rV2 common precursors and early GABA- and glutamatergic cells. Both Tal1 and Vsx2 cCREs contain conserved binding sites of Kr-like TFs, bHLH TFs, E2A, Ebf, E2F, NF-1, Pbx, and Sox TF families, and various HD TFs (Figure 3B–D, Figure 3—figure supplement 2C–E).
claims.evidence: This is based on footprinting analysis shown in the figures.

claims.claim: Four Sox TFs are expressed in early rV2 lineage cells (Sox2, Sox3, Sox4, and Sox11), which all may compete for the same binding sites in Tal1 +0.7 kb cCRE or Vsx2 –61 kb cCRE.
claims.source: For example, four Sox TFs are expressed in early rV2 lineage cells (Sox2, Sox3, Sox4, and Sox11), which all may compete for the same binding sites in Tal1 +0.7 kb cCRE or Vsx2 –61 kb cCRE (Figure 3C, Figure 3—figure supplement 2D).
claims.evidence: This is a speculation based on expression data and binding site analysis.

claims.claim: Identification of the common regulators of GABAergic fate selectors revealed 21 TFs in CO1–2 and 22 TFs in the GA1–2 cell groups.
claims.source: To further understand the mechanisms of the activation of lineage-specific selector expression, we asked which TFs commonly and specifically regulate the GABAergic selector TF genes Tal1, Gata2, and Gata3. Identification of the common regulators of GABAergic fate selectors revealed 21 TFs in CO1–2 and 22 TFs in the GA1–2 cell groups (Figure 3E).
claims.evidence: This is based on analysis of TF footprints at selector gene cCREs.

claims.claim: The common regulators between the stages are overlapping partially, with the TFs associated with the neurogenic cell cycle exit predominant in the common precursors (CO) and the postmitotic differentiation and the autoregulation network TFs showing activity later in the GABAergic precursors.
claims.source: Interestingly, the common regulators between the stages are overlapping partially, with the TFs associated with the neurogenic cell cycle exit predominant in the common precursors (CO) and the postmitotic differentiation and the autoregulation network TFs showing activity later in the GABAergic precursors.
claims.evidence: This is an inference based on the identity and timing of TF activity.

claims.claim: 12 TFs, including Ascl1, E2f1, Nkx6-1, and Vsx1 may regulate both GABA- and glutamatergic selectors in the CO1–2 cell group.
claims.source: We next asked which upstream regulators are common to both rV2 GABAergic (Tal1, Gata2, and Gata3) and glutamatergic (Vsx1 and Vsx2) fate selector genes. We identified 12 TFs, including Ascl1, E2f1, Nkx6-1, and Vsx1 that may regulate both GABA- and glutamatergic selectors in the CO1–2 cell group (Figure 3E, Figure 3—figure supplement 2F, genes indicated in bold).
claims.evidence: This is based on analysis of TF footprints at selector gene cCREs.

claims.claim: The distinct regulators of GABA- and glutamatergic fate selectors, aside from the lineage-specific autoregulatory functions of the selectors themselves, include Lhx1 and En2 in the GABAergic sublineage and Lhx4, Shox2, and Nhlh2 regulating Vsx2 expression in the glutamatergic lineage.
claims.source: The distinct regulators of GABA- and glutamatergic fate selectors, aside from the lineage-specific autoregulatory functions of the selectors themselves, include Lhx1 and En2 in the GABAergic sublineage (Lhx1-binding Tal1 +0.7 kb feature, Figure 3B), and Lhx4, Shox2, and Nhlh2 regulating Vsx2 expression in the glutamatergic lineage (Figure 3—figure supplement 2C-E).
claims.evidence: This is based on analysis of TF footprints at selector gene cCREs.

claims.claim: Footprints at Nkx6-1 TFBS were detected in the cCREs of all selectors in common precursors, but after onset of differentiation, they become restricted to the cCREs of Vsx2 and Vsx1 in the glutamatergic cells.
claims.source: Footprints at Nkx6-1 TFBS were detected in the cCREs of all selectors in common precursors, but after onset of differentiation, they become restricted to the cCREs of Vsx2 and Vsx1 in the glutamatergic cells.
claims.evidence: This is based on temporal analysis of TF footprints.

claims.claim: The Vsx2 –68.8 kb cCRE contains conserved GATA TF-binding sites.
claims.source: Interestingly, the Vsx2 –68.8 kb cCRE contains conserved GATA TF-binding sites (Figure 3—figure supplement 2E).
claims.evidence: This is based on binding site analysis shown in the figure.

claims.claim: Vsx1- and Vsx2-binding sites were found in the cCREs of Gata2 and Gata3, suggesting a mutual cross-regulation between the GABA- and glutamatergic selector genes.
claims.source: Conversely, Vsx1- and Vsx2-binding sites were found in the cCREs of Gata2 and Gata3, suggesting a mutual cross-regulation between the GABA- and glutamatergic selector genes.
claims.evidence: This is an inference based on the presence of binding sites.

claims.claim: Putative Vsx1-binding sites were detected in all three GABAergic fate selector genes, Tal1, Gata2, and Gata3, in the rV2 common precursors.
claims.source: Putative Vsx1-binding sites were detected in all three GABAergic fate selector genes, Tal1, Gata2, and Gata3, in the rV2 common precursors (Figure 3E, CO, CO1–2).
claims.evidence: This is based on binding site analysis shown in the figure.

claims.claim: Ascl1 and Neurog2 TFBS are found at the cCREs of both Tal1 and Vsx2.
claims.source: The proneural bHLH TFs appeared to contribute to the activation of the selector genes. Ascl1 and Neurog2 TFBS are found at the cCREs of both Tal1 (Figure 3C, D) and Vsx2 (Figure 3—figure supplement 2C, D).
claims.evidence: This is based on binding site analysis shown in the figures.

claims.claim: Neurog1 TFBS was bound at Vsx2 +20.5 and –61 kb cCREs in the rV2 common precursors.
claims.source: In addition, Neurog1 TFBS was bound at Vsx2 +20.5 and –61 kb cCREs in the rV2 common precursors (Figure 3—figure supplement 2C, D).
claims.evidence: This is based on footprinting analysis shown in the figure.

claims.claim: Several cell cycle-associated TFs may also contribute to the regulation of selector gene expression, including Sox2, Sox21, Insm1, Ebf1, Ebf3, and E2f1.
claims.source: Interestingly, several cell cycle-associated TFs may also contribute to the regulation of selector gene expression. Those include Sox2, Sox21, Insm1, Ebf1, Ebf3, and E2f1.
claims.evidence: This is a speculation based on the presence of binding sites and known TF functions.

claims.claim: E2f1 binds Tal1 cCREs +0.7 and +7 kb and is strongly expressed in the CO1–2, the common precursors of rV2 GABA- and glutamatergic cells.
claims.source: E2f1, and Ebf1–3-binding sites are located within the GC-rich areas (Figure 3B–D, Figure 3—figure supplement 2C–E). E2f1 binds Tal1 cCREs +0.7 and +7 kb and is strongly expressed in the CO1–2, the common precursors of rV2 GABA- and glutamatergic cells (Figure 3B).
claims.evidence: This is based on footprinting and expression data shown in the figure.

claims.claim: The expression of E2f1 declines after differentiation, while Ebf1–3 are expressed in common precursors (CO1–2) and maintained in differentiating neurons of both GABA- and glutamatergic sublineages (GA1–2 and GL1–2).
claims.source: The expression of E2f1 declines after differentiation, while Ebf1–3 are expressed in common precursors (CO1–2) and maintained in differentiating neurons of both GABA- and glutamatergic sublineages (GA1–2 and GL1–2) (Figure 3B–D, Figure 3—figure supplement 2C–E).
claims.evidence: This is based on expression data shown in the figures.

claims.claim: The scATAC-seq feature analysis suggested that Ebf1–3 TFs interact with Tal1 cCREs as well as Gata2 cCREs in both GABA- and glutamatergic cells.
claims.source: Interestingly, the scATAC-seq feature analysis suggested that Ebf1–3 TFs interact with Tal1 cCREs as well as Gata2 cCREs in both GABA- and glutamatergic cells (Supplementary file 3).
claims.evidence: This is based on feature linkage analysis.

claims.claim: The binding of Tal1, Gata2, and Gata3 at the Tal1 cCREs was supported by CUT&Tag.
claims.source: In addition to the footprint analysis, we analysed chromatin interactions of Tal1, Gata2, Gata3, Vsx2, Ebf1, and Insm1 in the E12.5 r1 by CUT&Tag (Figure 3—figure supplement 3, Figure 3—figure supplement 4, Figure 3—figure supplement 5). The binding of Tal1, Gata2, and Gata3 at the Tal1 cCREs was supported by CUT&Tag (Figure 3, Figure 3—figure supplements 3 and 4), consistent with the autoregulatory activity of the GABAergic fate selector genes.
claims.evidence: This is based on CUT&Tag data shown in the figures.

claims.claim: Tal1, Gata2, and Gata3 binding was detected at the Tal1 +23 kb cCRE, where scATAC-footprinting did not indicate binding at conserved sites.
claims.source: In addition to the Tal1 +0.7 and +40 kb cCREs, we detected Tal1, Gata2, and Gata3 binding at the Tal1 +23 kb cCRE, where scATAC-footprinting did not indicate binding at conserved sites (Figure 3A, C).
claims.evidence: This is based on CUT&Tag data compared with footprinting data.

claims.claim: Insm1 footprints were found in Tal1 cCREs –3.8 and +23 kb, while Insm1 CUT&Tag peaks were found at Tal1 +7, and +23 kb cCREs.
claims.source: The DNA binding of Insm1 and Ebf1 was also partially confirmed by CUT&Tag. Insm1 footprints were found in Tal1 cCREs –3.8 and +23 kb, while Insm1 CUT&Tag peaks were found at Tal1 +7, and +23 kb cCREs (Figure 3A, CUT&Tag Insm1).
claims.evidence: This is based on comparison of footprinting and CUT&Tag data.

claims.claim: scATAC-footprint was found at the conserved Ebf1 TFBS in Tal1 +77.4 kb cCRE and, by CUT&Tag, Ebf1 was found to interact with Tal1 +23 kb and Tal1 +40 kb cCREs.
claims.source: scATAC-footprint was found at the conserved Ebf1 TFBS in Tal1 +77.4 kb cCRE and, by CUT&Tag, Ebf1 was found to interact with Tal1 +23 kb and Tal1 +40 kb cCREs (Figure 3A).
claims.evidence: This is based on comparison of footprinting and CUT&Tag data.

claims.claim: Overall comparison of TF binding detected by scATAC-seq footprinting and by CUT&Tag indicates strong bias towards the same features.
claims.source: Overall comparison of TF binding detected by scATAC-seq footprinting and by CUT&Tag indicates strong bias towards the same features (Supplementary file 6).
claims.evidence: This is based on comparison of the two methods.

claims.claim: In our analysis, equivalent percentages range from 5.3% to 25.9%, depending on the TF.
claims.source: Earlier reports of corroborations between Cut&Run and footprinting have shown 9% (Lmx1b) and 30.5% (Pet1) of footprints having overlapping Cut&Run peak (Eastman et al., 2025). In our analysis, equivalent percentages range from 5.3% to 25.9%, depending on the TF.
claims.evidence: This is based on quantitative comparison of footprinting and CUT&Tag data.

claims.claim: An analysis of footprint positions in relation to CUT&Tag peaks indicates clear tendency of having most footprints towards the centre of the peaks.
claims.source: Additionally, an analysis of footprint positions in relation to CUT&Tag peaks indicates clear tendency of having most footprints towards the centre of the peaks (Figure 3—figure supplement 6), further validating eligibility of CUT&Tag and footprinting as corroborating methods.
claims.evidence: This is based on spatial analysis of footprints within CUT&Tag peaks.

results.result: Single-cell RNA-seq analysis of E12.5 ventral r1 reveals that rV2 cells arrange along pseudotemporal axes representing differentiating GABAergic and glutamatergic lineages, with selector TF genes (Tal1, Gata2, Gata3, Vsx1, Vsx2, Lhx4) strongly expressed at the lineage bifurcation point. Integration of scATAC-seq and scRNA-seq data shows that open chromatin features largely reflect gene expression patterns and enable pseudotemporal ordering of developing rV2 neurons.
results.evaluation: Claims C14-C16 are well-supported by scRNA-seq and scATAC-seq data presented in Figure 1 and supplementary figures. The pseudotemporal analysis, UMAP projections, and integration of chromatin accessibility with gene expression provide converging evidence for the developmental trajectories and cell type identities. The cluster similarity analysis (C16, Figure 1G) validates the correspondence between scRNA-seq and scATAC-seq datasets.

results.result: Chromatin accessibility analysis identifies 15 candidate cis-regulatory elements (cCREs) linked to Tal1 expression within its TAD. These cCREs show distinct temporal kinetics during GABAergic differentiation, with some (e.g., Tal1 +40 kb) accessible early and declining, while others (e.g., Tal1 +0.7 kb) maintain accessibility in late precursors. The Tal1 +23 kb cCRE contains spatially distinct binding sites for progenitor TFs (Nkx6-1, Ascl1) and early precursor TFs (Insm1, Tal1), suggesting distinct regulatory elements control activation versus maintenance of selector TF expression.
results.evaluation: Claims C17-C34 are supported by comprehensive scATAC-seq data, feature-to-gene linkage analysis (LinkPeaks with p<0.05), and temporal correlation with gene expression shown in Figure 2. The identification of distinct temporal patterns of cCRE accessibility (C29-C33) is well-documented in the heatmaps and correlation plots. The footprinting analysis (C32) provides mechanistic insight into the differential regulation. The inference about activation versus maintenance (C34) is reasonable given the temporal data.

results.result: The identified cCREs for Tal1, Gata2, Gata3, and Vsx2 overlap substantially with previously characterized enhancers from the literature, with 63.6-100% of known nervous system enhancers falling within the scATAC-seq features. Specific cCREs correspond to well-characterized regulatory elements including Tal1 midbrain/hindbrain enhancers, Gata2 autoregulation elements, and Gata3 CNS enhancer regions.
results.evaluation: Claims C20-C28, C37, and C41 are well-supported by literature comparisons documented in Supplementary file 4 and Figure 2—figure supplement 3B. The high overlap percentages (C41) validate the scATAC-seq approach. Each claim cites specific prior studies, and the correspondence between identified features and known enhancers strengthens confidence in the functional relevance of the cCREs.

results.result: Vsx2 expression is detected in common precursors (CO1) and increases in glutamatergic precursors (GL1-GL5). At the Vsx2 locus, intronic and distal features open concomitantly with expression activation, while promoter-proximal features show delayed accessibility in later glutamatergic precursors.
results.evaluation: Claims C35-C36 are supported by scRNA-seq expression data (Figure 2C) and temporal scATAC-seq analysis (Figure 2D). The differential timing of cCRE accessibility parallels the pattern observed for GABAergic selector genes, suggesting similar regulatory logic. The data presentation is clear and the temporal correlations are well-documented.

results.result: Sequence conservation analysis shows that scATAC-seq features are significantly more conserved than random genomic sequences (p<2.20e-16, Fisher's exact test), with conservation levels intermediate between exons and introns. This conservation pattern is consistent with a regulatory function for the identified chromatin features.
results.evaluation: Claims C38-C40 are supported by systematic conservation analysis using phastCons scores across vertebrate genomes (Supplementary file 5). The statistical testing is appropriate (Fisher's exact test), and the p-value is highly significant. The intermediate conservation level between exons and introns (C38) is expected for regulatory elements. The inference about regulatory function (C40) is reasonable but remains indirect evidence.

results.result: TF footprinting analysis identifies common and distinct regulators of GABAergic and glutamatergic selector genes. Both lineages share binding sites for Kr-like, bHLH, E2A, Ebf, E2F, NF-1, Pbx, Sox, and HD TF families. Twenty-one TFs commonly regulate GABAergic selectors in CO1-2 cells, with partial overlap with 22 TFs active in GA1-2 cells. Cell cycle-associated TFs (E2f1, Ebf1-3, Insm1, Sox2, Sox21) show footprints at selector gene cCREs, with E2f1 expression peaking at cell cycle exit and Ebf1-3 maintained during differentiation. Twelve TFs including Ascl1, E2f1, Nkx6-1, and Vsx1 may regulate both GABAergic and glutamatergic selectors in common precursors.
results.evaluation: Claims C42-C57 are supported by comprehensive footprinting analysis using TOBIAS with HOCOMOCO v12 motifs, filtered for conservation >0.5 and expression >1.2 (log1p). The data are presented in Figure 3 and supplementary figures with appropriate controls. The identification of common regulators (C44-C46) is based on systematic overlap analysis. The temporal patterns of TF expression (C55-C56) are validated by both scRNA-seq and in situ hybridization (Figure 4). The speculation about cell cycle-associated TFs (C54) is reasonable given their known functions, though direct functional validation is not provided.

results.result: CUT&Tag experiments validate TF binding at selector gene cCREs, with Tal1, Gata2, and Gata3 binding confirmed at Tal1 regulatory elements, supporting autoregulatory activity. Insm1 and Ebf1 binding is partially confirmed. Overall comparison shows 5.3-25.9% of footprints overlap with CUT&Tag peaks (depending on TF), comparable to published corroboration rates (9-30.5%). Footprints show clear tendency to localize toward the center of CUT&Tag peaks.
results.evaluation: Claims C58-C64 are supported by CUT&Tag data from E12.5 r1 samples (Figure 3—figure supplements 3-5, Supplementary file 6). The overlap percentages (C63) are within the range of published studies (Eastman et al., 2025), validating the methodology. The spatial analysis showing footprint enrichment at peak centers (C64, Figure 3—figure supplement 6) provides additional validation. However, some antibodies (anti-Insm1, anti-Tead2, anti-Vsx2) lack prior ChIP validation, which is a limitation noted in the methods. The partial confirmation (C59-C61) is appropriately qualified.

results.result: In situ hybridization validates that Insm1, Sox4, E2f1, Ebf1, and Tead2 are expressed in the ventricular zone of ventrolateral r1 at E12.5, overlapping with Tal1 expression. Quantitative analysis along the apical-basal axis shows that Insm1, E2f1, and Tead2 peak slightly closer to the ventricular surface than Tal1, while Ebf1 follows Tal1 closely and Sox4 peaks more basally. These spatial patterns match the temporal expression patterns from scRNA-seq, consistent with these TFs having a role in initiating Tal1 expression.
results.evaluation: Claims C65-C71 are well-supported by RNAscope in situ hybridization data (Figure 4A-F) with quantitative analysis using StarDist segmentation and LOESS smoothing across three biological replicates. The spatial patterns along the apical-basal axis (C66-C68) are clearly documented with confidence intervals. The correspondence between spatial (in situ) and temporal (scRNA-seq) patterns (C69) strengthens the interpretation. The inference about a role in Tal1 initiation (C71) is reasonable given the temporal precedence, though direct functional evidence is not provided.

results.result: ChromVAR analysis reveals genome-wide enrichment of Sox, NeuroD1, and Nfia/b/x motifs in accessible regions of rV2 progenitors and precursors, consistent with their roles in temporal gene regulation and cell cycle exit. Nhlh1/2, NeuroD2, Bhlhe22, Ebf1-3, Pou3f4, and Lhx5 motifs become accessible in common precursors, preceding Gata2/3 and Tal1 motif accessibility in GABAergic neurons. For Tal1, Gata2, and Gata3, motif accessibility closely follows RNA expression, with the TAL1.H12CORE.0.P.B motif (a 19-bp E-box-GATA composite) showing the most GABAergic-specific activity pattern.
results.evaluation: Claims C72-C78 are supported by ChromVAR analysis (Figure 5) with appropriate filtering (correlation >0.5, p<0.01). The genome-wide patterns (C72, C74) are consistent with the cCRE-specific footprinting results. The temporal progression of motif accessibility (C74) provides additional support for the regulatory hierarchy. The identification of the TAL1.H12CORE.0.P.B motif as most GABAergic-specific (C77) is data-driven. The inference about heteromeric Gata2-Tal1 complex binding (C78) is reasonable given the motif composition but remains speculative without biochemical validation.

results.result: Integration of footprinting, conservation, and CUT&Tag data identifies 3948 Tal1 targets, 780 Gata2 targets, and 721 Gata3 targets. About half are differentially expressed between GABAergic and glutamatergic neurons, though most targets are lowly expressed (only 30% above 0.5 log1p). GSEA shows Tal1 targets are expressed in both lineages, while Gata2 and Gata3 targets are enriched in GABAergic neurons. Target genes with proximal selector TF-bound features (0-5 kb) show higher expression variability and more cell-type-specific patterns than distally regulated genes. Highly expressed targets are enriched for inhibitory interneuron markers.
results.evaluation: Claims C79-C88 are supported by systematic target gene identification using multiple criteria (footprints, conservation >0.5, CUT&Tag peaks, LinkPeaks |z-score|>2, p<0.01) as shown in Figure 6A. The GSEA analysis (C82-C83) is appropriate and clearly shows differential enrichment patterns. The expression variability analysis stratified by distance (C85-C86) provides insight into regulatory logic, though the conclusion about proximal regulation (C86) should be tempered by the fact that many genes have multiple regulatory inputs. The CellMarker enrichment (C88) validates the biological relevance of the targets. The low expression of many targets (C81) is a limitation but is transparently reported.

results.result: Analysis of target gene overlap reveals that genes commonly regulated by Tal1, Gata2, and Gata3 are exclusively overexpressed in the GABAergic lineage and include autoregulatory network genes (Gata2, Tal1, Zfpm1, Lmo1). The GABAergic phenotype genes (Gad1, Gad2, Slc32a1) are regulated by Gata2 and Gata3. Tal1 appears involved in Notch signaling (Pdzk1ip1, Hes5) and interacts with glutamatergic-specific genes (Lhx4, Nkx6-1), possibly repressing them in GABAergic precursors. Cross-regulation between lineages is suggested, with Gata3 potentially repressing Vsx2 in GABAergic cells and Vsx2 potentially repressing Lmo1 in glutamatergic cells.
results.evaluation: Claims C89-C91 are supported by target gene overlap analysis (Supplementary file 8, Figure 7). However, claims C92-C95 involve speculation about regulatory effects (activation vs. repression) that cannot be definitively determined from chromatin occupancy data alone, as acknowledged in the discussion. The proposed cross-repression (C95) is reasonable given the mutually exclusive expression patterns and prior functional studies cited (C113-C117), but direct evidence for repression versus failed activation is not provided. Functional validation experiments would be needed to confirm these regulatory relationships.

results.result: Nkx6-1 directly regulates the spatial expression pattern of selector TFs in the region where it is expressed, but is not sufficient for their activation, which requires cell cycle exit. TFs E2f1, Ebf1, and Insm1 temporally control selector TF expression and connect it to cell cycle exit.
results.evaluation: Claims C96-C98 are supported by the integration of multiple data types: spatial correlation of Nkx6-1 expression with selector TF activation (C96), footprinting showing Nkx6-1 binding at selector cCREs (C48), temporal expression patterns showing selector activation only in postmitotic cells (C97), and footprinting plus expression data for E2f1, Ebf1, and Insm1 (C98). The inference about direct regulation by Nkx6-1 (C96) is strengthened by the footprinting data, though functional validation would be ideal. The connection to cell cycle exit (C98) is well-supported by the temporal expression patterns and known functions of these TFs.

results.result: E2f1, typically known as a cell cycle progression factor, shows a complex expression pattern with low levels in proliferative progenitors and peak expression at cell cycle exit, consistent with dose-dependent effects on cell cycle regulation. Ebf1 and Insm1 have been previously associated with cell cycle exit and neuronal differentiation. These findings suggest that mechanisms guiding cell cycle exit also contribute to selector TF activation and neuronal phenotype adoption.
results.evaluation: Claims C99-C103 are supported by expression data (C101: Figure 4, scRNA-seq) and citations to prior literature (C100, C102). The observation that E2f1 peaks at cell cycle exit (C101) is consistent with the dose-dependent model cited in C100. The inference about cell cycle exit mechanisms contributing to selector TF activation (C103) is reasonable given the temporal correlation and known TF functions, though it remains somewhat speculative without direct functional manipulation.

results.result: Autoregulation is a prominent feature of Tal1, Gata2, and Gata3 expression in the developing brain, as evidenced by footprinting and CUT&Tag showing binding of these TFs at their own regulatory elements. This is supported by prior loss-of-function studies showing that Gata2 and Gata3 are required for Tal1 maintenance (but not initiation), and reciprocally, Tal1 is required for Gata2 and Gata3 maintenance. These TFs appear to work together in maintaining their expression, potentially as a physical complex involving Lmo1.
results.evaluation: Claims C104-C110 are well-supported by multiple lines of evidence: footprinting and CUT&Tag data showing autoregulation (C107: Figure 3, C58), prior loss-of-function studies (C108-C109: Lahti et al., 2016), and the identification of Lmo1 as a common target (C90). The speculation about a physical complex (C110) is reasonable given prior biochemical studies (Ono et al., 1998) and the co-regulation patterns, though direct biochemical evidence in this system is not provided. The positive feedback model (C104-C105) is well-established in developmental biology.

results.result: Tal1, Gata2, and Gata3 interact with glutamatergic lineage-specific TF genes (Vsx2, Lhx4), suggesting cross-regulation between lineages. The time of co-expression of GABAergic (Gata2/3) and glutamatergic (Vsx1/2) selectors is short. Prior studies show that Vsx1 represses Tal1 in zebrafish, while Tal1 and Gata3 overexpression reduce Vsx2 expression in mouse and chicken spinal cord. Negative feedback and cross-repression between the Tal1-Gata2-Gata3-Lmo1 network and Vsx2 would ensure robust selector TF expression patterns.
results.evaluation: Claims C111-C117 are supported by target gene analysis (C111: Figure 7), scRNA-seq temporal data (C113-C114), and multiple prior functional studies in spinal cord (C115-C117). The short co-expression window (C113) supports the cross-repression model. However, the speculation about negative feedback (C112) cannot be definitively confirmed from the chromatin occupancy data alone, as TFs can have context-dependent activating or repressive effects. The model is plausible and consistent with the data, but functional validation in the r1 system would strengthen the conclusions.

results.result: Combinatorial function of Tal1, Gata2, and Gata3 is important for adopting GABAergic identity, supported by similar fate transformations in mutant embryos. However, Tal1 activity is less biased toward GABAergic genes than Gata2 and Gata3. The selector TFs regulate not only GABAergic subtype-specific genes but also genes expressed more broadly, suggesting their function extends beyond neurotransmitter phenotype specification to enabling overall cellular function.
results.evaluation: Claims C118-C122 are supported by target gene analysis (C120-C121: Figure 6, GSEA) and prior loss-of-function studies (C119: Lahti et al., 2016). The differential enrichment patterns between Tal1 versus Gata2/Gata3 (C120) are clearly shown in the GSEA plots. The observation that many targets are expressed in both lineages (C121) is well-documented. The inference about broader cellular functions (C122) is reasonable given the target gene diversity, though it remains somewhat speculative without detailed functional characterization of individual targets.

results.result: Background and translational context: The ventral rhombomere 1 produces GABAergic and glutamatergic neuron precursors important for behavioral control. Tal1, Gata2, and Gata3 are required for GABAergic identity and inhibit glutamatergic identity. Failure of Tal1-dependent neuron development causes ADHD-like behaviors in mice. The anterior brainstem is important for behavioral control, and variants in regulatory regions important for brainstem neuron differentiation may predispose to neuropsychiatric disorders.
results.evaluation: Claims C1-C13 and C123-C125 provide background context supported by prior literature (C7-C11: multiple citations) and the authors' previous work (C9, C124: Morello et al., 2020a,b). These claims establish the biological and translational significance of the study. The speculation about genetic variants and neuropsychiatric disorders (C125) is reasonable given the demonstrated link between brainstem development and behavior (C9, C124), though it remains speculative without human genetic evidence.

results.result: Summary of main findings: Tal1, Gata2, and Gata3 are activated by highly similar mechanisms connected to regional patterning, cell cycle exit, and neuronal differentiation. After activation, they are linked by auto- and cross-regulation and interact with glutamatergic TFs. GABAergic genes appear under combinatorial control of Tal1, Gata2, and Gata3, unlike glutamatergic-specific genes.
results.evaluation: Claims C2-C5 summarize the major findings of the study and are supported by the comprehensive data presented throughout the manuscript. C3 is supported by the cCRE analysis showing similar regulatory logic (Results section on cCRE kinetics), C4 by the footprinting and CUT&Tag data (Figure 3, target analysis), and C5 by the target gene overlap analysis (Figure 6-7, Supplementary file 8). These summary claims accurately reflect the supported results.

results.result: The authors used scRNA-seq and scATAC-seq to identify and characterize rV2 cell populations along pseudotemporal axes representing GABAergic and glutamatergic differentiation lineages. Selector TF genes (Tal1, Gata2, Gata3, Vsx1, Vsx2, Lhx4) were strongly expressed at the lineage bifurcation point, and open chromatin features reflected gene expression patterns.
results.evaluation: Reviewers explicitly praised the 'high quality of the datasets' and noted that the authors 'use an extensive set of computational approaches to identify temporal patterns of chromatin accessibility, TF motif binding activities (footprints), gene expression.' The integration of scRNA-seq and scATAC-seq data to place cells in pseudotemporal order is accepted without critique.

results.result: The authors identified candidate cis-regulatory elements (cCREs) at the Tal1, Gata2, Gata3, and Vsx2 loci through scATAC-seq feature analysis, showing temporal patterns of accessibility that correlate with gene expression. Many identified cCREs overlap with previously characterized enhancers, and distinct regulatory elements may be responsible for activation versus maintenance of selector TF expression.
results.evaluation: Reviewers stated that 'state of the art computational methods were convincingly implemented to identify candidate regulatory elements' and that the work provides 'predictions about upstream regulators, candidate accessible CREs, and DNA binding motifs.' The identification of cCREs and their temporal dynamics is accepted as a core contribution.

results.result: The identified chromatin features show significant sequence conservation compared to introns and exons, consistent with a regulatory role. Previously characterized enhancers of Tal1, Gata2, Gata3, and Vsx2 largely overlap with the identified scATAC-seq features (63.6-100%).
results.evaluation: Reviewers noted the 'high quality of the datasets' and the convincing implementation of computational methods. The conservation analysis and overlap with known enhancers support the validity of the identified regulatory elements, and no concerns were raised about these findings.

results.result: Footprinting analysis identified common and distinct TF binding patterns at selector gene cCREs, including binding sites for Kr-like TFs, bHLH TFs, E2A, Ebf, E2F, NF-1, Pbx, Sox, and various HD TFs. Common regulators of GABAergic selectors include 21 TFs in CO1-2 and 22 TFs in GA1-2, with TFs associated with cell cycle exit predominant in common precursors and autoregulation network TFs active later. Distinct regulators include Lhx1 and En2 for GABAergic and Lhx4, Shox2, and Nhlh2 for glutamatergic lineages.
results.evaluation: Reviewers acknowledged that the authors 'use an extensive set of computational approaches to identify temporal patterns of chromatin accessibility, TF motif binding activities (footprints)' and that 'their conclusions and predictions are largely well supported.' The footprinting analysis is treated as a valid method for predicting upstream regulators.

results.result: CUT&Tag experiments validated TF binding predictions from footprinting analysis. Tal1, Gata2, and Gata3 binding at Tal1 cCREs was confirmed, as was partial confirmation of Insm1 and Ebf1 binding. Overall comparison showed strong bias towards the same features between footprinting and CUT&Tag (5.3-25.9% overlap), with footprints tending to localize toward the center of CUT&Tag peaks.
results.evaluation: Reviewers noted the use of 'a combination of single-cell and bulk sequencing data, prediction and validation' as a strength. The CUT&Tag data is treated as validation of the footprinting predictions, and no concerns were raised about the concordance between methods.

results.result: In situ hybridization validated the expression of candidate upstream regulators (Insm1, Sox4, E2f1, Ebf1, Tead2) in the ventricular zone of ventrolateral r1 at E12.5, overlapping with Tal1 expression. Quantitative analysis showed that Insm1, E2f1, and Tead2 expression peaks slightly closer to the ventricular surface than Tal1, while Ebf1 follows Tal1 closely but is expressed earlier, consistent with a role in initiating Tal1 expression.
results.evaluation: One reviewer specifically noted that 'Insm1, Sox4, E2f1, Ebf1 and Tead2 TFs might be the strongest upstream candidates for future testing of Tal1 activation given the extensive analyses of their spatiotemporal expression patterns relative to Tal1, presented in Fig 4.' This indicates acceptance of the in situ validation and its interpretation.

results.result: ChromVAR analysis showed that accessible genomic regions in rV2 cells are enriched in Sox, NeuroD1, and Nfia/b/x TF-binding motifs, and that Nhlh1/2, NeuroD2, Bhlhe22, Ebf1-3, Pou3f4, and Lhx5 motifs are accessible in common precursors preceding Gata2/3 and Tal1 motif accessibility. For Tal1, Gata2, and Gata3, accessibility at most TFBSs closely follows TF RNA expression, with the TAL1.H12CORE.0.P.B motif showing the most GABAergic-specific activity.
results.evaluation: Reviewers noted the 'extensive set of computational approaches' and that 'many of the TFs with footprints in selector gene cCREs had a genome-wide activity pattern consistent with a regulatory function.' The ChromVAR analysis is treated as supporting evidence for the regulatory network predictions.

results.result: The authors identified 3948 Tal1, 780 Gata2, and 721 Gata3 target genes using integrated evidence from footprints, TFBS conservation, and CUT&Tag. Tal1 targets are expressed in both GABAergic and glutamatergic neurons, while Gata2 and Gata3 targets are overexpressed in GABAergic precursors. Target genes with proximal selector TF-bound features (0-5 kb) show the most cell-type-specific patterns. Common targets of all three GABAergic selectors include autoregulatory and GATA co-factor network genes (Gata2, Tal1, Zfpm1, Lmo1), while GABAergic phenotype genes (Gad1, Gad2, Slc32a1) are regulated by Gata2 and Gata3.
results.evaluation: Reviewers stated that 'the authors have achieved their aim of making predictions about upstream and downstream selector TF regulatory networks' and that 'their conclusions and predictions are largely well supported.' The target gene analysis is treated as a valid prediction of downstream effectors, though reviewers note it has not been experimentally tested.

results.result: The authors propose that Nkx6-1 directly regulates the spatial expression pattern of selector TFs but is not sufficient for their expression, which requires cell cycle exit. TFs E2f1, Ebf1, and Insm1 temporally control selector TFs and connect their expression to cell cycle exit, suggesting that mechanisms guiding neurogenesis also contribute to selector TF activation and neuronal phenotype adoption.
results.evaluation: Reviewers noted that 'their conclusions and predictions are largely well supported' and specifically highlighted the analysis of upstream regulators including E2f1, Ebf1, and Insm1. The mechanistic interpretation linking cell cycle exit to selector TF activation is accepted as a reasonable inference from the data.

results.result: The authors propose that autoregulation is a prominent feature of Tal1, Gata2, and Gata3 control in the developing brain, with these TFs working together (potentially as a physical complex involving Lmo1) to maintain their expression through positive feedback. They also propose cross-regulation between GABAergic and glutamatergic selector genes, with negative feedback ensuring robust selector TF expression patterns.
results.evaluation: Reviewers stated that the authors 'predict auto- and cross-regulatory interactions for maintenance of selector expression' and that 'their conclusions and predictions are largely well supported.' The autoregulatory and cross-regulatory mechanisms are accepted as reasonable predictions based on the binding data and prior literature.

results.result: The authors conclude that combinatorial function of Tal1, Gata2, and Gata3 is important for adopting GABAergic identity, with differences in target gene specificity: Tal1 activity is less biased toward GABAergic genes than Gata2 and Gata3. The selector TFs regulate not only subtype-specific genes but also genes expressed more broadly, suggesting their function extends beyond neurotransmitter phenotype to overall cellular function.
results.evaluation: Reviewers noted that 'the work clearly illustrates the daunting gene regulatory complexity likely at play in controlling rV2 transmitter fate' and that the authors' conclusions about combinatorial regulation are 'largely well supported.' The interpretation of target gene data is accepted without critique.

results.result: The authors' primary conclusions are that Tal1, Gata2, and Gata3 genes are activated by highly similar mechanisms connected to regional patterning, cell cycle exit, and neuronal differentiation; that after activation they are linked by auto- and cross-regulation as well as interactions with glutamatergic TFs; and that GABAergic neuron genes are under combinatorial control of these three TFs.
results.evaluation: Reviewers stated that 'the authors have achieved their aim of making predictions about upstream and downstream selector TF regulatory networks; their conclusions and predictions are largely well supported.' These core conclusions are treated as the main contributions of the study and are accepted by reviewers.

results.result: The authors speculate that variants in genomic regions important for gene regulation during brainstem neuron differentiation could lead to altered brain development and predisposition to neuropsychiatric disorders.
results.evaluation: While reviewers acknowledged the work 'may also contribute to understanding of neuropsychiatric traits and disorders,' this speculative claim about human disease relevance is not directly evaluated. One reviewer noted 'the study does not go as far as to experimentally test the transcription factor network,' indicating the work remains at the prediction stage.

comparisons.comparison: Perfect agreement on claims C14-C16. Both evaluations find the scRNA-seq and scATAC-seq data integration well-supported, with reviewers praising the 'high quality of the datasets' and OpenEval noting the converging evidence from pseudotemporal analysis and UMAP projections.

Strong agreement on cCRE identification (C17-C19, C29-C34). OpenEval provides detailed technical validation while peer reviewers accept the 'state of the art computational methods' for identifying candidate regulatory elements. Peer review R2 covers a broader claim set (C17-C37) that overlaps with multiple OpenEval results.

Both address literature validation of cCREs (C20-C28, C37). OpenEval emphasizes specific overlap percentages and prior study citations, while peer reviewers accept the computational methods as 'convincingly implemented' for identifying candidate regulatory elements.

Both support differential timing of cCRE accessibility (C35-C36). OpenEval provides specific evidence from temporal analysis, while peer reviewers accept this as part of the broader temporal pattern identification using computational approaches.

Strong agreement on conservation analysis (C38-C40). OpenEval details the phastCons statistical testing while peer reviewers accept the conservation findings as supporting the validity of identified regulatory elements. Peer R3 also covers C41 which OpenEval addresses in R3.

Perfect agreement on footprinting analysis (C42-C57). Both find the TF motif binding predictions well-supported. OpenEval provides detailed technical validation while peer reviewers acknowledge the 'extensive set of computational approaches' for identifying TF motif binding activities.

Perfect agreement on CUT&Tag validation (C58-C64). Both treat the CUT&Tag data as successful validation of footprinting predictions. OpenEval notes some antibody validation limitations while peer reviewers emphasize the strength of combining 'prediction and validation.'

Perfect agreement on in situ hybridization validation (C65-C71). Both find the spatial expression patterns well-supported. Peer reviewers specifically highlight these TFs as 'strongest upstream candidates for future testing,' while OpenEval notes the correspondence between spatial and temporal patterns.

Perfect agreement on ChromVAR analysis (C72-C78). Both accept the genome-wide motif accessibility patterns as supporting the regulatory network predictions. OpenEval notes the heteromeric complex inference remains speculative, while peer reviewers accept it as part of the broader computational validation.

Strong agreement on target gene identification (C79-C88). Both find the systematic target identification well-supported. OpenEval provides detailed technical criteria while peer reviewers note the authors 'achieved their aim of making predictions about downstream selector TF regulatory networks.'

Partial agreement on regulatory relationships (C89-C95). OpenEval rates these claims as UNCERTAIN due to speculation about activation vs. repression that cannot be determined from chromatin data alone. Peer reviewers accept the predictions as 'largely well supported' but acknowledge they have not been experimentally tested.

Strong agreement on upstream regulation and cell cycle exit (C96-C98, C103). Both find the mechanistic interpretation linking Nkx6-1, cell cycle exit, and selector TF activation well-supported by the integration of multiple data types.

Agreement on cell cycle exit mechanisms (C99-C103). Both accept the temporal correlation between E2f1 expression and selector TF activation as reasonable inference, though OpenEval notes it remains somewhat speculative without direct functional manipulation.

Strong agreement on autoregulation (C104-C110). Both find the positive feedback model well-supported by footprinting, CUT&Tag, and prior literature. OpenEval notes the physical complex speculation lacks direct biochemical evidence in this system, while peer reviewers accept the predictions as largely well-supported.

Strong agreement on cross-regulation (C111-C117). Both find the cross-repression model supported by target gene analysis and prior functional studies. OpenEval notes the negative feedback cannot be definitively confirmed from chromatin data alone, while peer reviewers accept the predictions with the caveat that experimental testing has not been performed.

Perfect agreement on differential target regulation (C118-C122). Both find the GSEA analysis and target gene diversity well-supported. Peer reviewers note the work 'clearly illustrates the daunting gene regulatory complexity,' while OpenEval accepts the broader cellular functions inference as reasonable.

Both address the speculative claim about neuropsychiatric disorders (C125). OpenEval rates the background claims as SUPPORTED but notes C125 remains speculative without human genetic evidence. Peer reviewers rate this as UNCERTAIN, acknowledging the potential contribution but noting the work remains at the prediction stage.

Perfect agreement on core study conclusions (C3-C5). Both find these summary claims well-supported by the comprehensive data. Peer reviewers state the authors 'achieved their aim' and 'conclusions are largely well supported,' while OpenEval confirms these claims accurately reflect the supported results.
